planting.note: Scarify and stratify seed before spring sowing, or set out nursery plugs into dry, well-drained prairie soil.

directions: Scarify and stratify seed before spring sowing, or set out nursery plugs into dry, well-drained prairie soil where this diminutive shrub forms a tidy, low mound rather than the taller thickets of its relatives. Short spikes of fragrant purple flowers with prominent orange anthers appear in late spring and are worked heavily by bumblebees, leafcutter bees, and other native pollinators drawn to the sweet scent. It is especially well suited to short-grass and mixed-grass prairie restorations of the Dakotas, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, where its compact size keeps it from overwhelming smaller neighboring wildflowers. Established plants are extremely drought tolerant thanks to a deep taproot and rarely need irrigation once past their first season.

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto prepared prairie or savanna soil in fall for natural cold stratification over winter, or dormant-seed in early spring.

directions: Broadcast seed onto prepared prairie or savanna soil in fall for natural cold stratification over winter, or dormant-seed in early spring. This cool-season bunchgrass produces distinctive nodding, hairy seed heads by early summer and stays a soft blue-green through the growing season, filling the structural gap left by warm-season prairie grasses that green up later. It provides nesting material and cover for ground-nesting bees and ample seed for sparrows and other grassland birds, and its fibrous roots help stabilize soil in mixed prairie plantings. It tolerates drier, calcareous soils better than many native grasses, making it valuable on thin or gravelly sites.

planting.note: Sow stratified seed shallowly in fall or divide established clumps in early spring, siting in dry to mesic prairie or rocky glade plantings with excellent drainage.

directions: Sow stratified seed shallowly in fall or divide established clumps in early spring, siting this diminutive iris relative in dry to mesic prairie or rocky glade plantings with excellent drainage. Despite the name it is not a true grass but produces flattened, grass-like fans of foliage topped in late spring by small pale blue to white star-shaped flowers with a yellow throat. The flowers open only in sunny weather and attract small native bees and syrphid flies seeking pollen, since they offer no nectar reward. It is short-lived but self-sows readily in open, disturbed prairie soil, so plant it among sparser companions rather than dense turf-forming grasses.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall to allow its two-stage dormancy to break naturally over successive seasons, or plant divisions from an established colony in spring.

directions: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall to allow its two-stage dormancy to break naturally over successive seasons, or plant divisions from an established colony in spring for quicker results. Creamy-white, five-petaled flowers rise on wiry stems above deeply lobed basal leaves in early summer, followed by the namesake cylindrical, cottony seed heads that persist into winter and provide nesting fluff for birds and native bees. It thrives in dry prairie, sandy savanna, and disturbed open ground, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies over time. The nectar-poor flowers rely mainly on pollen-collecting bees and flies, making it a useful early-summer companion to nectar-rich prairie species.

planting.note: Sow seed outdoors in fall on lean, dry prairie soil and expect a long, patient wait; this deep-taprooted species is difficult to transplant.

directions: Sow seed outdoors in fall on lean, dry prairie soil and expect a long, patient wait, since this deep-taprooted species is difficult to transplant and slow to reach blooming size from seed. In mid-spring it produces clusters of brilliant orange-yellow tubular flowers covered in fine silvery hairs, among the earliest and showiest blooms of the tallgrass prairie. The flowers are pollinated chiefly by long-tongued bees, including several species that specialize on Lithospermum, and its taproot helps it persist through drought once established. Because of its slow start, interplant it with faster-establishing companions and avoid disturbing the soil around its root once seedlings appear.
